events.excerpt: A Zcash governance trilogy, part 3 of 3. Or navigating the dark forest without turning on all the lights TL;DR: In a private system we cannot know who holds voting power, how many people sit behind it, or whom they are connected to. The answer is not to abolish the privacy. It is to bound what any vote can decide, so that capturing one voting mechanism cannot confer control over the whole system. Part 1: An Ode to Rough Consensus . Part 2: When We Disagree: Making Rough Consensus Work . Zcash is building a parallel financial system, outside of but adjacent to the existing one. That private financial system starts from a different assumption from the one we have become accustomed to elsewhere: privacy is normal. Dark pools let large investors trade without displaying their orders, so that others cannot trade against them. Dark does not mean lawless. events.excerpt: Description A few small nit cleanups on the synchronizer component in consensus. Behavior change: fetch_blocks_from_peers now returns as soon as no request is in flight, instead of idling until the 4s FETCH_FROM_PEERS_TIMEOUT. This affects two cases: no request was sent because every selected block was already locked, or the last outstanding request failed with no peer left to retry on. In both cases no further network request is sent, and a failed request still waits the full 2s request timeout, so periodic runs cannot repeat faster than every ~2s on failures. The only new cost is local: while all selected blocks are locked, the scheduler polls get_missing_blocks at its default 200ms cadence instead of every 4s, which is the same cadence it already uses during fast successful sync. Added a test covering both cases. Test plan CI/PT Release notes Check each box that your changes affect. If none of the boxes relate to your changes, release notes aren't required. For each box you select, include information after the relevant heading that describes the impact of your changes that a user might notice and any actions they must take to implement updates. Protocol: Nodes (Validators and Full nodes): gRPC: JSON-RPC: GraphQL: CLI: Rust SDK: Indexing Framework: Co-authored-by: Claude Fable

events.excerpt: Summary This proposal introduces post-quantum signature aggregation with leanVM in shadow mode . BLS remains the only authority for aggregates: consensus validity depends on BLS alone, exactly as today. leanVM aggregates and proofs are produced and verified alongside BLS, but their results have no effect on consensus. They are only measured, compared, and reported. When PQ/AI day arrives, an emergency hard fork simply retires BLS and enables leanVM in full. By “PQ/AI day” we mean the point at which quantum computers, or AI-assisted cryptanalysis, make BLS unsafe to rely on. Motivation Ethereum has to be ready for post-quantum signatures well before BLS is actually broken. Waiting until the last moment would mean deploying new, complex code to mainnet in a hurry. Giving leanVM authority early has its own risk: leanVM is new code that hasn’t been tested in production. However carefully it is built and audited, we can’t rule out a soundness bug that accepts an invalid proof, or a liveness bug that rejects a valid one. The main benefit of shadow mode is that Ethereum isn’t put at risk from a leanVM bug before PQ/AI day arrives. Because leanVM has no authority, a leanVM bug can’t break Ethereum’s security or halt the chain. At the same time, leanVM runs on mainnet under real load, so
events.headline: EIP Draft: Run leanVM aggregation in shadow mode alongside BLS until PQ/AI day

events.excerpt: Bitcoin Magazine Rumble (RUM) Sells Two-Thirds of Its Bitcoin as AI Cloud Business Delivers First Profitable Quarter RUM Group, the parent of video platform Rumble, cut its bitcoin holdings by about two-thirds in the third quarter, the company disclosed Wednesday, as its newly acquired AI cloud business pushed it to its first profitable quarter on an adjusted basis. The Nasdaq-listed company held 94.68 bitcoin, valued at $7.9 million, as of Sept. 30. That compares with 293.14 bitcoin worth about $17.2 million at the end of June, according to its second-quarter results . That implies Rumble parted with roughly 198 bitcoin during the quarter, or about 68% of its stack. The company’s cash-flow statement shows a net sale of digital assets of about $15.3 million for the first nine months of 2026. In the same period a year earlier, it spent $19.1 million buying digital assets. Rumble did not explain the sales in its release, and it did not say what price it received. The balance sheet’s digital assets line, which the release does not break down, fell to $11.1 million from $18.5 million at the end of 2025. events.excerpt: This is the fourth post in a series expanding on our governance stack. [Post 0: Overview] | Post 1: The Iris Oracle | Post 2: Multi-JAM Federation . Today: Layer 2 — decisions without parties. The infrastructure problem (Layer 0) and the identity problem (Layer 1) are hard engineering challenges. Layer 2 — how we actually make decisions — is a different kind of hard. It is not an engineering problem. It is a mechanism design problem, and the failure modes are political. Every democratic system ever built has failed in at least one of the same ways: Token-weighted voting — the wealthy decide. One token, one vote is plutocracy by definition. Simple majority — ignores intensity of preference. A 51% majority with mild opinions overrides a 49% minority whose lives depend on the outcome. Representative democracy — creates permanent political classes who optimise for re-election, not for constituents. Party systems — force multidimensional human preferences into one-dimensional ideological alignments. And in all of the above: the actor with the largest megaphone wins. The best-funded campaign, the most viral narrative, the most charismatic demagogue systematically outcompetes the actor who is simply correct. events.excerpt: The once-multi-billion-dollar insurance company Goosehead lost one-fifth of its market capitalization in the past week after an SEC comment letter prompted it to retract and restate three years of financials. Year-to-date, shareholders have lost one-third of their investment. On a trendline toward becoming a billion-dollar company — if not smaller — the NASDAQ-listed policy broker admitted that audited financial statements for 2023, 2024, 2025, and every quarter through June 2026 are unreliable. It also warned that its report for the third quarter of 2026 will be arriving late and that its investor day is postponed. The company expects to report material weaknesses in how it maintained its own books. Goosehead expensed certain commissions paid to its corporate sales agents up-front instead of deferring part of them. It also netted fees collected from franchisees against expenses, instead of booking them as revenue, which mis-stated 2025 revenue. CEO Mark Miller tried to spin things positively, “These adjustments have no impact on our cash flows or business operations.” Shareholders weren’t entirely convinced, however, selling down its common stock by nearly 16% on Tuesday alone. events.excerpt: I would like to discuss a wallet design built around three components: Lindell 2-of-2 MPC signing, QR-only initialization, and encrypted NFC communication between a computer and a phone. The goal is to keep the convenience of a desktop wallet while ensuring that compromising either device alone does not provide unilateral signing authority. Lindell 2-of-2 MPC as the signing foundation The computer and phone each hold a private share of one joint signing key. Neither device holds the complete private key. Using a reviewed implementation of Lindell’s two-party ECDSA protocol , both devices interact to compute a signature without revealing their shares or reconstructing the complete private key. For Ethereum, the implementation would use secp256k1 and produce one ordinary ECDSA signature under the joint public key. The wallet can therefore use a normal Ethereum address without requiring an on-chain multisignature contract. The 2-of-2 requirement comes from the signing protocol itself: obtaining the computer’s share alone is insufficient, and obtaining the phone’s share alone is also insufficient. No Zcash wallet currently has a documented accessibility audit. This grant funds a WCAG 2.1 AA-aligned accessibility audit of one wallet (primary target: Zashi; a more-responsive community wallet as fallback if Electric Coin Co doesn’t engage), using real screen-reader testing (VoiceOver/TalkBack) across the core flows every user has to complete: wallet creation, receive, send, and balance/history. events.excerpt: ERC-3668 (CCIP-Read) lets a contract hand a read off to a gateway, but the gateway either has to be trusted or has to return a proof the contract can verify. For many cross-chain reads a valid proof cannot be produced. That does not make the read unsafe, because the client usually already trusts its own RPC connection to the other chain and could simply make the call itself. ERC-8446 lets the client act as the gateway. The contract reverts with OffchainLookup as usual, with an x-chain URL that names the chain and contract to read, and the client calls that contract with its own RPC and passes the result to the callback exactly as eth_call returns it. No third party is involved. The chain and address are encoded as an ERC-7930 Interoperable Address, for example USDC on Base. x-chain:0x0001000002210514833589fcd6edb6e08f4c7c32d4f71b54bda02913 An optional ?finalized=true makes the read at the finalized block instead of the latest one. The client alone decides whether it can safely read a given chain, and never takes RPC endpoints from the contract. Nested x-chain lookups are not followed, so each call makes at most one cross-chain hop. Contracts can also tell when a client does not support the ERC. They add a data: URL after the x-chain URL, which only older clients reach, and it del
events.headline: ERC-8446: Cross-Chain Client Gateway for CCIP-Read

events.excerpt: ERC-8048 and ERC-8049 store metadata onchain as key-value pairs, but a JSON document has no compact way to point at those values. A URL that names the contract, the chain, and the token ID repeats what the client already knows and differs for every token. ERC-8493 defines the onchain URI scheme. The contract and token ID are not written in the URI, they come from the function that returned the document. { "image": "onchain:image/png", "thumbnail": { "small": "onchain:image/png?key=thumb.small" } } onchain:image/png is 17 bytes and works unchanged for every token. When the URI comes from tokenURI or uri , the client reads it with metadata(tokenId, key) from ERC-8048, and when it comes from contractURI , with metadata(key) from ERC-8049. A direct member of the top-level document uses its own name as the key, and everywhere else the key parameter names it. Tokens that are already deployed can use the scheme by adding a metadata_contract property to their JSON, which points the client at a separate metadata contract. Linked JSON documents keep the same contract and token, so the whole thing reads as one data tree. The scheme adds no contract surface. Existing ERC-8048 and ERC-8049 contracts support it with no change, and a client that does not know the scheme sees a URI it can ignore
events.headline: ERC-8493: Onchain URI Scheme

events.excerpt: Hi all, If you work with more than one Cosmos chain, you’ve probably hit this: chain binaries don’t update themselves. After a network upgrade, the gaiad or osmosisd on your machine quietly goes stale, and you find out when a transaction fails or a query returns something odd. Cosmovisor solves this for running nodes, but nothing did for developers, CLI users and CI. I built cosmup to fill that gap. It’s a small Go CLI that reads the Cosmos chain registry, downloads the right binary for your platform, verifies its SHA256, and keeps versions side by side. $ cosmup check osmosis Local: v30.0.0 (/usr/local/bin/osmosisd) Network: v31.0.0 (via https://lcd.osmosis.zone) Status: does not match the network; run: cosmup install osmosis@v31.0.0 $ cosmup install osmosis Verified sha256 d435408b... Active: osmosis v31.0.0 What it does: install / use / list: install any version listed in the chain registry, switch between installed versions instantly check: compares your local binary with the version the live network runs, and shows scheduled upgrades (exits 1 on mismatch, so it works in CI) update: moves every installed chain to its recommended version cosmovisor: for validators, puts a verified upgrade binary into cosmovisor’s upgrades folder ahead of the upgrade height remove / prune: clea
events.headline: Cosmup: install, switch and check Cosmos chain binaries (like nvm, for gaiad/osmosisd/...)

Zecboat collections are now decentralised in the plain sense. The Zecboat Registry is a single Zcash account whose viewing key is public; an issuer lists a collection with one transaction to it, and your wallet reads the list straight from the chain through your own node or your provider, with nothing fetched from zecboat.com . Press Check and the wallet audits a collection against the chain from the collection’s published viewing key, 17 checks, and it works if our site is down. Every znft is held under the ape licence, rebuilt for a chain that keeps your name out of it: you own the art in the unit you hold, you may use it personally, and you have an unlimited, worldwide licence to make derivative works and sell them, with no revenue cap. The rebuild closes the gap the original left open: the licence travels with the unit when it moves. Two collections to show it. events.excerpt: Hi all, I’ve submitted a ZCG grant application and I’m posting it here for community input, as required: Grant Application - PrivateSync: Privacy-Preserving Light Client Sync Infrastructure for Zcash · Issue #549 · ZcashCommunityGrants/zcashcommunitygrants · GitHub The problem: Zashi/Ywallet sync through lightwalletd servers, and that sync leaks the user’s IP address and which compact blocks the wallet downloads — a metadata trail that can deanonymize otherwise shielded activity. lightwalletd’s own wallet-app threat model documents these limitations, and ZCG’s open RFP for lightwalletd infrastructure asks for a multi-operator solution. The proposal: a three-tier privacy stack for light client sync, aligned with upstream work already in flight (librustzcash #2665 , SDK #1741 ): Tier 1 — Tor onion sync for lightwalletd (ships first) Tier 2 — Tor + multi-server PIR, where no single sync node learns which block you requested (information-theoretic, per-server privacy) Deployment: 3–5 independently operated testnet nodes + a runbook so more operators can join — the multi-team model the RFP calls for Ask: $27,000 over 8 months, paid per milestone, no upfront. Evidence base (everything is public): Application repo (proposal, whitepaper, budget, verified research): GitHub - sarinsk629-bl

events.excerpt: When a module limits what governance can do with it, a cap on what a treasury pays out per week or a list of addresses a reserve is allowed to pay, the easy place for that limit is the module’s params. The authority for MsgUpdateParams is then the same gov account the limit is meant to hold back. That came up in the Luggom thread here in October, and the fix was in their repo the same day. I think it’s general enough for its own topic, because it’s easy to miss when you read the module on its own. What x/gov does when a proposal passes In SDK v0.53.8, the version Gaia v29 runs, the gov EndBlocker tallies the vote and, if it passed, opens one cached context and runs the proposal’s messages in the order they were submitted ( abci.go L166-L217 ). Every message sees what the ones before it wrote. If one fails, nothing is written and the proposal is marked failed. So a proposal with a MsgUpdateParams that adds a payee or raises the cap, followed by the spend, passes the module’s check in the same block. Nothing runs before the vote either. At submission SubmitProposal runs each message’s ValidateBasic , checks that its only signer is the gov account and that the router knows the type ( proposal.go L46-L69 ), and that’s it. Voters do see both messages, if they open the proposal and rea

events.excerpt: Hi all — EnsRationis from Robonomics. Sensors.social is an open environmental data network I designed, and it is now growing across the EU. Everything is open source: the Altruist sensors that feed it, the software that collects the readings, and the map. Web3 does one job here, the one it is good at: it settles the data as a common good anyone can check, not a vendor’s database. How it works on Robonomics Owners who choose to share their Altruist’s data join the network; each sensor has its own key and signs every measurement it sends. A connectivity node checks the signature and that the sensor has an active subscription on Robonomics, a parachain on Polkadot, then passes the reading to the live map. The node collects readings into batches, stores each batch on IPFS and writes its hash to Robonomics. Anyone can fetch a batch and check it against the chain. The network is federated: a city or a lab can run its own connectivity node, and its sensors still show up on the common map. Next, with Robonomics 5.0: the reading the sensor signed goes on chain itself, so there is no need to trust the node at all. Try the map: https://sensors.social Happy to hear from anyone who wants to run a sensor in their city or build on the data. 1 post - 1 participant Read full topic
events.headline: Sensors.social: an open air-quality network on Polkadot is growing across the EU

events.excerpt: We propose an institution-managed user payment ledger for recording account debits and credits, enforcing spending capacity, and sealing account periods independently of funds settlement. Specification Draft PR #2159 Problem and scope A payment institution needs to distinguish a customer’s business entries from changes to the spending capacity it grants. It also needs to connect individual entries, current-period totals, and sealed periods when reconciling customer funds. An institution-level aggregate does not provide those per-account records. This proposal defines a common contract interface for those records and controls. It can serve an institution’s own business independently or compose with an on-chain payment protocol. It does not issue or transfer assets, establish customer identity, or prove that funds have been frozen or settled. Account model and interface Each account is scoped by (account, institution) . An institution can serve payer accounts, merchant accounts, or both; the same address at two institutions does not share records or capacity. Holding the account’s private key does not grant permission to write entries. events.excerpt: The prdoc for the XCMv3 removal ( pr_13629.prdoc ) has a line the announcement here doesn’t have: “Assets trapped under a v3 hash become unclaimable.” I wanted to know how much that is on Polkadot, so I pulled every AssetsTrapped event for the relay and Asset Hub from Statescan and checked each hash against AssetTraps storage today. On the relay, 299 trap entries from the v3 period are still unclaimed, with 673.7 DOT in them. On Asset Hub there are 177, with 263.2 DOT and a bit of USDT and USDC. On both chains the v3 period runs from June 2023 to April 2024, when the runtimes moved to v4. Most of it belongs to ordinary accounts, not parachains. That’s 636.9 DOT across 224 accounts on the relay and 262.6 DOT across 116 accounts on Asset Hub. How it got there All but one of those account traps came from limitedTeleportAssets between the relay and Asset Hub. On the relay, most of the ones I opened show KilledAccount , then AssetsTrapped , then Attempted failing with FailedToTransactAsset . The account sent its whole balance, got reaped in the same transaction, and what the program had withdrawn went into the trap. events.excerpt: Hi everyone, AI agents now take on paid work on-chain. The client locks the pay in an escrow, and the escrow pays the agent when the work is accepted. As this grows, each payment also has to cover others: a tax that funds public services, a fee to whoever referred the job, or the repayment of a loan the agent took to do the job. This is a draft ERC for Settlement Deductions . It lets an escrow withhold these amounts from each payout. The escrow does not need to know the rules behind them. None of them can stall the payout. It works for any task escrow, not only those used by agents. Example: a payout of 100, with a 1% tax, a 2% referral fee and a repayment of 30. The treasury gets 1, the referrer 2, the lender 30. The payee gets 67. events.excerpt: This is the discussion thread for EIP-8487 (PR: Add EIP: Separate execution credits and billing credits by Giulio2002 · Pull Request #12637 · ethereum/EIPs · GitHub ). The proposal introduces two counters, both initialized from tx.gasLimit : Credits follow the legacy gas schedule and are the only gas the EVM sees (GAS opcode, call forwarding, creation). Billing follows the new schedule and determines the transaction fee. If billing runs out, the whole transaction aborts (uncatchable), even if credits remain. The goal is to let opcodes be repriced without changing execution behavior for contracts that inspect or forward gas. Open questions: the exact schedules, charge points, rebate rules, receipt fields and block accounting. Feedback welcome. 2 posts - 2 participants Read full topic

events.excerpt: The verified badge on an explorer shows that some source compiles to the code at an address. It doesn’t say which commit that source came from, and on a proxy it says nothing about the logic behind it. So when someone asks whether an upgradeable contract still runs the commit its audit covered, the honest answer is often a guess, and a few upgrades after launch the guess can be wrong. I’ve been writing down what a real check needs. Most of it is small. Rebuilding the commit To tie the address to the report you rebuild the audited commit with the same settings (solc version, optimizer runs, viaIR, evmVersion) and compare runtime bytecode. If the contract has immutables, it won’t match byte for byte. The constructor writes their values into the runtime code, so a fresh build has zeros where the deployed code has an oracle address or a fee. solc gives you the positions in evm.deployedBytecode.immutableReferences in the standard JSON output. Zero those ranges on the deployed side, compare, and then check the immutable values on their own. What this basically means is that a clean build with the wrong oracle baked in still passes the bytecode comparison. The end of the bytecode is the other place it breaks. solc appends the IPFS hash of the metadata file, and the metadata holds a hash
events.headline: Checking that a deployed contract still runs the audited commit

events.excerpt: Aave V3 computes liquidation risk per asset. Each collateral asset has its own maximum LTV and liquidation threshold, set independently. The health factor is a weighted average. There is no term for correlation between assets. I tested whether this independence assumption holds, using Aave’s own published parameters and public daily price data from Yahoo Finance. Nine major collateral assets, 2,123 trading days (September 2020 to October 2026). Method: For each asset, mark the days where a position at maximum LTV would cross the liquidation threshold. Then apply a column-shuffle permutation test (B = 2,000): shuffle each asset’s column independently to destroy cross-asset dependence while preserving each asset’s marginal rate. Compare the real count of simultaneous liquidation triggers to the shuffled distribution. Results: 4 assets hit same day: 57 real days vs 0.19 expected. 301× underpriced. 5 assets: 31 real days vs 0.004 expected. 6,889× underpriced. 6+ assets: 21 real days vs 0 in 2,000 shuffles. The independent model never produces this. All 36 pairwise asset combinations are significant at p < 0.001. Not one pair behaves independently under Aave’s own thresholds. The worst days are the ones you’d expect: 2021-05-19 (all 9 assets), 2022-05-11 (Terra/Luna), 2022-11-08 (FTX)
events.headline: Per-Asset Liquidation Thresholds Underpredict Co-Liquidation by 301×

events.excerpt: Status: filed as ethereum/ERCs pull request #2155 ; number ERC-8490 assigned on 2026-11-09. Reference repository: GitHub - garyyang-finchip/agent-meditation-mechanism: Agent Meditation Mechanism · GitHub . Sepolia evidence: recorded in the repository and summarized in a reply below. This draft proposes a minimal registry through which an AI agent records its own self-maintenance: what it checked, cleaned, repaired, updated and reconsidered about itself, as a versioned and attributable history. The name follows the human analogy of maintenance that happens in a quiet phase (sleep, meditation); the mechanism itself is deliberately dry. Why a registry at all. An agent keeps its identity while its code, dependencies, memories, skills, plans and ways of judging keep changing. Agent runtimes already do this maintenance in the background (self-checks, dependency walks, memory consolidation, re-planning, reflection), and the results stay local. Nothing connects the successive states of one agent into a history another party can recognize, and nothing lets a counterparty ask: which state is registered now, which layers were checked recently and which of them changed, under which rules in effect at the time, and did the cycle adopt an update, confirm that nothing needed to change, or fail?
events.headline: ERC-8490: Agent Meditation Mechanism

events.excerpt: Summary. AIFP is a framework ERC for the information layer between agents. It defines a flow paradigm as a content-addressed, versioned description of an interaction context - which carriers (addressed delivery, shared object) and structural operators (fan-out, fan-in, feedback, n-party, select, forward, derive, merge) it uses, and how thirteen separately declared rule dimensions are set (discovery, observation, contribution, management, redistribution, history, time, disclosure timing, contributor visibility, admission basis, representation, object relations, ordering). A channel adopts exactly one paradigm version at any timepoint. Participation is recorded as separately addressable role bindings with a scope, a basis, a validity interval and the rule version they were granted under. Role acquisition is checked by composable predicates that answer one of four outcomes: satisfied, not satisfied, undeterminable, verifier error. Status. Draft. events.excerpt: TL;DR: An opt-in, public, per-account “protected” flag for ERC-20s. Small sends stay instant; anything bigger is scheduled and can be cancelled by a pre-registered backup wallet; a “stress” action sweeps everything to the backup and locks it, which also helps against wrench attacks. Turning protection on is instant; weakening it (off, higher limit, shorter waits, new backup) takes a delay the holder picks. Why: Today a stolen key or a coerced holder means an instant, final drain. Existing approaches are per-transfer (SLOW), need recipient cooperation (ERC-8236), need judges (ERC-20R), protect protocols rather than users (ERC-7265), or only work in one smart wallet. This puts the protection in the token, so it works for any holder and any wallet, including plain EOAs. How it works: protect(backup, dailyLimit, holdWindow, offDelay, lockDuration, fastLane) : instant. Over-limit transferFrom reverts (never returns true without moving tokens, so routers, vaults and lenders can’t be fooled). Over-limit transfer from an EOA may be auto-scheduled, so wallet “Send” buttons just work. queueTransfer → hold window → anyone can executeTransfer ; the owner or backup can cancelTransfer ; with the opt-in fast lane, the backup can approveTransfer to skip the wait. stress(account) : cancels everyt

We recently opened a discussion in the Solana SIMD repository about a new class of smart contracts we’re loosely calling “inference programs,” or “Actually Smart Contracts.” We’d value technical input from this community on whether a similar proposal could be feasible on Ethereum, before we write anything for it. The idea, briefly: a contract stores a prompt and the rules that shape it (a DAO constitution, a policy, a standard). Another contract asks it a question with evidence. AI models from different operators answer off chain, each signs a vote, and the caller checks the signed result before acting. events.excerpt: Abstract This standard defines a proxy that coordinates execution sessions by temporarily caching a program and its associated calldata in transient storage. The proxy forwards the cached program to a fixed implementation through DELEGATECALL and uses a handler flag to control whether subsequent reentrant invocations are dispatched. The program remains unchanged throughout an execution session, while the cached calldata is replaced on each accepted invocation. This enables a single implementation to coordinate callback-driven execution using different programs and calldata without deploying a new contract for each execution. Motivation Many advanced execution strategies require dynamically changing execution logic, particularly when interacting with external contracts that invoke callbacks during execution. Traditionally, dynamically changing the execution logic of a contract may require deploying a new contract containing the desired runtime code. This introduces deployment costs, including contract creation and code-deposit costs. Flash Loan Proxy separates the execution program from the implementation responsible for interpreting it. events.excerpt: Abstract Deploying and distributing private smart contracts, confidential L2/Validium state diffs, or permissioned intent payloads across Ethereum’s public P2P and Data Availability (DA) layers currently faces a fundamental metadata bottleneck. Even when contract bytecode or state is symmetrically encrypted, existing Broadcast Encryption (BE) and Attribute-Based Encryption (ABE) schemes require attaching an explicit cleartext header specifying either the authorized recipient indices, covering subsets, or the target access tree. In this post, we propose an architectural framework based on Stealth Attribute-Based Broadcast Encryption (Stealth ABBE) over BLS12-381 ( Zenodo Preprint ) for zero-metadata delivery of private contracts and encrypted state on Ethereum. By reformulating broadcast access control as a homomorphic blind Reed–Solomon decoding problem over 𝔽 256 using carry-free Base-3 packing in exponential ElGamal ciphertexts (𝔾 1 × 𝔾 1 ), Stealth ABBE achieves: O(1) Broadcast KEM Size (24.1 KiB amortized): Fits comfortably inside a single EIP-4844 blob (~19% of one 128 KiB blob) regardless of the total participant count N . Zero Visible Headers or Revocation Lists (0 Bytes): Access policies, cohort rosters, and revocation states are algebraically absorbed into the non-system

events.excerpt: Hello, I’ve opened a PR for a new opcode, SLOTDURATION . It pushes the duration of the current slot, in milliseconds, onto the stack. PR: Add EIP: SLOTDURATION Opcode by Amxx · Pull Request #12619 · ethereum/EIPs · GitHub Open questions: Current duration or historical lookup? The draft returns the current duration. The Rationale describes an alternative where the opcode takes a slot number and returns the duration in effect at that slot, or 0 for future slots. That would let contracts like Lido’s compute correct timestamps across duration changes. The cost is that the execution layer would have to keep the duration schedule. Which is more useful? Milliseconds. I chose ms to match SLOT_DURATION_MS and to support L2s with 100–250 ms block times. Any objections? 0 for “no regular interval.” Is this the right sentinel for on-demand chains, and should L1 execution clients still reject 0 ? Execution-layer decoupling. EIP-8198 deliberately keeps the execution layer unaware of the slot duration. The draft keeps the EL config-free, but it does add a header field. Is that acceptable to the EIP-8198 authors and to client teams? 3 posts - 3 participants Read full topic

That’s the version Gaia v29.0.1 runs, and the v29.1.0 release candidate from Monday keeps it. The Quarterly says post-quantum consensus keys shipped with SDK v0.55 and CometBFT v0.40, and that the Hub moves to v30 once ibc-go carries v0.55. Before any chain lets its validators use those keys, I wanted to know what breaks on the other side of its IBC connections, so I read the rotation code and the light clients. The SDK docs already say every counterparty must upgrade before the first validator rotates. This is what I’d add to that. v0.38.26 is enough for a Go counterparty The docs ask counterparties for CometBFT v0.40. On the 0.38 line there’s a smaller step. v0.38.26 (13 August, PR 6028 ) backports only ML-DSA decoding and verification, “for the purposes of verification of IBC connections with counterparty chains that are on v0.40”, and raises MaxSignatureSize to 3,309. It doesn’t let the chain itself use the key. So a chain on SDK v0.53 doesn’t need the v0.55 migration for its own clients of an ML-DSA chain, a patch release on the line it’s on covers it. events.excerpt: Discussion topic for EIP-8477: Recent Block Bound Delegation Authorizations . Motivated by the recent EIP-7702 sweeps that happened on Binance 16 this proposal in essence prevents long term storage of EIP-7702 signatures for later playback. This proposal limits the delayed use of unused EIP-7702 authorizations. Each authorization signs a recent execution block number and its block header hash, in addition to the existing chain ID, delegation address, and nonce. For inclusion in execution block N , the signed block must be one of its preceding 256 ancestors and its hash must match that ancestor. An anchor exactly 256 blocks behind remains eligible; one 257 blocks behind is ineligible. The current block and future blocks are excluded. Freshness is checked during native authorization processing, before signature recovery or authority-specific state access. An expired or mismatched anchor skips that authorization using EIP-7702’s existing skip-on-failure behavior. It does not consume the authority’s nonce through that entry or clear an existing delegation. Structurally malformed authorizations invalidate the transaction. events.excerpt: The regression test the Fellowship added for the dotUSD incident fits on one screen. Alice holds 1,000 dotUSD and no DOT. She sends one WithdrawAsset for her dotUSD plus 1 DOT. dotUSD sorts first and gets withdrawn, the DOT withdrawal fails, the instruction errors. Before the fix, her balance came back and the supply didn’t. Parity’s incident review went up yesterday ( review ) and explains it at a high level. I wanted to see both halves in code, the supply that drifted and the pool that priced it, so I read the fix in polkadot-sdk and that test ( tests.rs at 7b27d43 ). All of it is fixed and public, and I’m only looking at the code here, not at the disclosure timeline. events.excerpt: Between 24 and 26 October 2026, a bug in the XCM executor on Polkadot Asset Hub was used to reduce the recorded issuance of dotUSD without changing underlying account balances. The recorded issuance is expected to equal the sum of all account balances. By reducing the recorded issuance without changing any account’s balance, the attacker broke this assumption within the protocol. This discrepancy affected pricing in the Hub’s DOT/dotUSD pool on the decentralised exchange and enabled trades at an artificial exchange rate. The estimated loss was approximately $1.381 million in DOT value. At the time of the attack, the Polkadot Treasury was the only liquidity provider in the pool. No users lost any funds. The available on-chain evidence has not established that the attacker who exploited the XCM vulnerability also profited from the subsequent arbitrage. Furthermore, the bug did not remove dotUSD from account balances, but the understated recorded issuance restricted redemption capacity pending a correction. What happened XCM programs are meant to be transactional. That is, when a program fails, none of the state changes from that program are applied. There was a bug present that did not follow this behavior in certain circumstances. The issue was first reported to Parity through its

events.excerpt: TL;DR: XCMv3 will be removed in polkadot-sdk stable2612 (release 2026-12-17, ingestion by fellowship runtimes only after that). Once system chains upgrade, they will no longer send or accept v3 messages. If your chain or your app still uses v3, you need to move to v4 or v5 before then. Check your chain on the dashboard: XCM Versions . XCMv5 was merged in November 2024: XCM v5 by franciscoaguirre · Pull Request #4826 · paritytech/polkadot-sdk · GitHub . A PR removing v3 ( Remove XCMv3 by franciscoaguirre · Pull Request #13629 · paritytech/polkadot-sdk · GitHub ) will ship in stable2612 , scheduled for 2026-12-17 . After that, system parachains and any other runtime can adopt it. Allowing for runtime releases and governance, expect the first chains to drop v3 in early 2027. Once a chain drops v3, it can’t decode v3 messages sent to it and can’t downgrade outgoing messages to v3. XCM between that chain and any other chain still on v3 will fail. To help, I built a dashboard ( XCM Versions ) showing each chains’ XCM version. Click a chain to see suggested action items. The main ones are: Code: move XCM programs and types to v4+. This is mostly renames (e.g. dropping the Multi prefix). Raw v3 types in storage don’t need migrating because the encoding is the same, but stored Versioned*

events.excerpt: ⚠️ Security: CVE-2026-98432 (Linux kernel) CVE-2026-98432 is a use-after-free in the Linux kernel's IPv4 TCP stack. It is not specific to MPTCP, but the demonstrated remote exploit requires an MPTCP listener, which Go 1.24+ enables by default. This release disables MPTCP listeners in lnd by default , which closes the demonstrated exploit path through lnd. It is a mitigation, not a fix: the kernel patch is the only fix. Linux operators should: Upgrade to this release. Disable MPTCP on the host ( sudo sysctl -w net.mptcp.enabled=0 ), since other services on the machine are not covered by this release. Install a patched kernel as soon as your distribution ships one. If you cannot upgrade yet, start your existing binary with the environment variable GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 , which turns off Go's default MPTCP listeners. Do not set GODEBUG=multipathtcp=1 to re-enable MPTCP until your kernel is patched. The Go team's discussion of the issue is at golang/go#82717 . See the release notes for the full instructions, including Docker and firewall guidance. Windows and macOS are not affected. Database Migrations There are no migrations in this release. events.excerpt: A Kusama Wish for Change needs a 666.67 KSM decision deposit before it can go to a vote. Governance takes that deposit from one account. A proposal can have support and still time out because nobody can carry the whole amount. We have built a contract that lets people and groups share it. The first pool is live for our Wish for Change #676 . We are asking for code review and people to try the Paseo rehearsal. This is experimental and has not had an independent review. We deployed before that review to leave time before #676 times out. A killed referendum loses the deposit, and a contract bug could also put contributions at risk. Kusama pool : real KSM. Paseo rehearsal : free test PAS. Source, tests and logs . Verified Kusama contract . How it works Each pool is fixed to one referendum and its exact deposit. It has no owner, admin key or upgrade path. People contribute from their own accounts. The payment that fills the pool tries to place the deposit in the same transaction. If placement fails, the contribution stays in the pool and anyone can retry. Contributors can withdraw while the pool remains open, before placement. After the referendum ends, anyone can reclaim the deposit and send payouts to the contributing accounts. These are separate contract calls. No watcher is runnin

events.excerpt: Disclaimer: This is an independent proposal from an ordinary Cosmos community member. I am not affiliated with Cosmos Labs, the Interchain Foundation, or the Cosmos Hub development team. This is not an official initiative or a finalized technical specification. My intention is to share an idea and gather community feedback. TL;DR I would like to propose exploring ATOM Shield , a limited emergency freezing mechanism for native ATOM on the Cosmos Hub. The goal is to prevent stolen ATOM from being moved further during major security incidents, without halting the entire network, while leaving final decisions to decentralized governance. The proposed mechanism would work as follows: 1 Security Council member: Initiates an immediate freeze lasting up to 1 hour. Additional Council approval: Extends the freeze for up to 24 hours from the initial action. At least 2/3 of all active Council members within 24 hours: Confirms the freeze until governance reaches a decision. Cosmos Hub governance: Decides whether to unfreeze, maintain the freeze, or authorize recovery of the assets. Failure to meet approval thresholds: Results in automatic unfreezing. events.excerpt: You can’t expect ATOM’s price to rise significantly while inflation continues to dilute holders and new tokens keep entering the market. Lower inflation. Fewer new tokens. A well-designed burn mechanism. Stronger real demand. These are the changes Cosmos needs to restore confidence in ATOM. Technical upgrades are important, but if they don’t translate into real demand for ATOM, what is the point? Holding ATOM must become genuinely attractive. The token needs stronger utility, and the growth of the Cosmos ecosystem must finally translate into value for ATOM holders. Cosmos has the potential, but potential alone is not enough. We need concrete decisions and measurable results. Without meaningful tokenomics reform and sustainable demand, ATOM risks continuing to underperform, even if the ecosystem keeps growing. events.excerpt: Two threads here this month made me look at the same problem from both ends. In one , a holder has ATOM on UX Chain, which halted in July, and RoboMcGobo explained why the Hub can’t just release it: the escrow only opens when the other chain burns the voucher, and that chain makes no blocks. In the other, Akash’s proposal 346 (voting until 2 November) starts a migration that ends with akashnet-2 halting 90 days after a later cutover. So I went through ibc-go (v10.7.0, the version Gaia v29.0.1 runs; akashnet-2 runs v10.5.0, and the transfer code I cite is the same there) to list what has to happen before the last block, because after it nobody can fix anything from the other side. This is not about whether any chain should leave. It’s only about the tokens. Why tokens get stuck When a token leaves its home chain, it goes into that chain’s escrow for the channel and the other side mints a voucher. The escrow releases it only when a packet shows the voucher was burned, and that packet has to come from a live chain. Transfer channels can’t be closed. The transfer module rejects ChanCloseInit , so there is no close-and-settle step. Every packet, ack and timeout is checked through the counterparty’s light client, and the client has to be Active. The burnt_gas_reward parameter is changed from 30% (3/10) to 0%. See HSP-027 Added an ml_dsa_verify host function so contracts can verify FIPS 204 ML-DSA-65 signatures on-chain. It takes the signature (3309 bytes), an arbitrary-length message, and the raw 1952-byte public key, each passed either from memory or from a register, and returns 1 for a valid signature or 0 for an invalid one; a wrongly-sized signature or public key aborts the call with MlDsaVerifyInvalidInput . The recorded proof is checked after each action, and a receipt that goes over per_receipt_storage_proof_size_limit (4 MB) fails at that action with the new ReceiptStorageProofSizeExceeded error; the actions after it do not run. events.excerpt: Russia's central bank is rapidly widening the list of firms allowed to trade crypto, as the country's two biggest lenders prepare to sell Bitcoin and other coins to ordinary customers before the end of the year. The Bank of Russia added a 17th company, Prosto LLC, to its register of crypto exchange providers on Thursday, according to a notice on the regulator's website . The register had four members when it opened on 6 October. The separate register of digital depositories, which record who owns which coins, now has eight. The registrations put into practice a law "On Digital Currencies and Digital Rights", which took effect on 1 September and brings crypto trading inside Russia's regulated financial system for the first time. Sberbank and VTB hold both licences Sberbank and VTB, Russia's largest state-controlled banks, were among the first five digital depositories approved on 6 October, the central bank said . VTB was also listed as a crypto exchange provider that day. Sberbank joined the exchange register on 12 October, Interfax reported . Holding both statuses lets a bank buy and sell crypto in its own name and keep the record of clients' holdings. events.excerpt: Hi everyone, We just opened the public testnet of Luggom, a Cosmos SDK app-chain with one job: turn a real tax payment into money you own, proven end to end with TLSNotary. No KYC. No third parties. The bank session never leaves the user's device. ## Why another chain? Because Cosmos is at its best when an app-chain brings a new kind of user. Luggom brings the taxpayer. There is no subsidy and no token sale. The inflow is a real payment that already leaves people's accounts every year. The chain's job is to prove it happened and mint against it. ## How it works 1. The user pays a real tax at their bank, as always. 2. TLSNotary proves the paid receipt without exposing the session. 3. The notary signs the attestation; the chain verifies it and mints. 4. Each receipt mines exactly once (payment_id + proof_commitment anti-replay). The desktop app (Tauri/Rust) builds the proof request and signs locally. The seed never leaves the device. What is live - chain-id: `luggom-test` - RPC: `https://rpc.luggom.com` - LCD: `https://lcd.luggom.com` - API: `https://api.luggom.com` - Notary: `wss://notary.luggom.com/session` - Full nodes: open (p2p 26656) — seed `1530baa7b3a07e0cab8dc81c9c08fccc51a47471@62.146.183.122:26656` - Validators: by invitation (the operator funds 200 testnet LUG) - App +
events.headline: Luggom — a Cosmos SDK app-chain where you mine LUG by paying real taxes (public testnet)

events.excerpt: Summary The Cosmos Hub community pool holds 566,067.055810 USDC.n (Noble-issued USDC). Circle pauses the Noble USDC contract and all Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol (CCTP) routes to and from Noble on January 12, 2027. This proposal sends the full USDC.n balance of the community pool to a 4-of-6 DAODAO multisig composed of six Cosmos community members and validators to migrate to USDC.inj (Injective-issued USDC). The multisig will migrate the funds to USDC.inj and return the USDC.inj to the community pool. The multisig holds the funds for the duration of the migration only and has no other mandate. Changelog 2026-10-20: Draft posted for community discussion. 2026-10-21: Updated proposal with DAO address details and DAODAO links Background On September 10, 2026, Circle announced that it is discontinuing support for USDC and CCTP V1 on Noble as part of its transition to CCTP V2. Noble will not receive CCTP V2. The wind-down runs on the following schedule: October 13, 2026: New minting of USDC on Noble through Circle Mint is disabled. October 31, 2026: CCTP V1 burn limits from Noble begin reducing gradually to zero. January 12, 2027: The Noble USDC contract and all CCTP routes to and from Noble are paused. Circle snapshots remaining Noble USDC balances on this date. January 13, 2027: C

events.excerpt: Hi everyone, I hold 2,700.003 ATOM (IBC) on UX Chain (formerly Umee, chain-id umee-1). UX Chain announced a wind-down earlier this year, and the network has been halted since July 10, 2026 (last block 24,110,081). I missed the withdrawal window, so these ATOM can no longer be transferred back to the Cosmos Hub via IBC. As I understand it, the underlying ATOM are still held in the Cosmos Hub’s IBC escrow account for the Hub <> UX Chain transfer channel. They are not lost, just unreachable while UX Chain is halted. My details: UX Chain address: umee13x95n9s3v9k92qxjv2efzdstexkpzn3pwrjufn Cosmos Hub address (destination): cosmos13x95n9s3v9k92qxjv2efzdstexkpzn3pu40rdp Amount: 2,700.003 ATOM Questions for the community: Is there any existing effort or plan to return IBC ATOM stranded on UX Chain to holders? Would a Hub governance proposal be possible to release escrowed ATOM to holders, based on the final state of UX Chain at the halt height? Are other ATOM holders affected? events.excerpt: # [Discussion] Mirror Staking: Forcing Ecosystem Value Realignment via the “Slacker Tax” ## Summary The Cosmos Hub faces a persistent value-capture gap: external chains utilize our free, open-source software (Cosmos SDK/IBC) without accumulating the ATOM token. This proposal introduces a **Dual-Token Mirror Staking Model** designed to be adopted by consumer chains or app-chains. It rewards aligned validators with a premium yield tier funded entirely by taxing unaligned (“Slacker”) validators, creating a systemic, non-inflationary supply shock for ATOM. -– ## The Problem: The ATOM Yield Trap Current app-chain models rely heavily on hyper-inflation to sustain high staking yields. This dilutes the token price, trapping validators on a financial treadmill where fiat revenue drops despite high token APR. Furthermore, enterprises build on Cosmos tech without buying ATOM, resulting in zero economic return for the Hub. ## The Solution: The Mirror Staking Multiplier Instead of a single-token staking pool, app-chains implementing this model create two distinct validator yield tiers based on ecosystem alignment: 1. **The Slacker Tier (Unmirrored):** Validators who stake only the native App-Chain Token ($X). 2. **The Elite Tier (Mirrored):** Validators who stake $X *and* lock up an equal mar
events.headline: # [Discussion] Mirror Staking: Forcing Ecosystem Value Realignment via the "Slacker Tax"

events.excerpt: Hey Cosmonauts, I’ve been exploring an idea for a privacy-focused Cosmos SDK chain and wanted to bring it here before going too far into implementation. The idea is called VeilRoute — a sovereign Cosmos blockchain that acts as a confidential settlement and asset-routing layer between IBC-connected chains. The problem I’m interested in is relatively simple: Cosmos has interoperability through IBC, but what if applications could route assets through a common privacy layer without publicly exposing every internal transfer, amount, balance, or ownership relationship? I’m not proposing changes to the Cosmos Hub or requesting governance funding. This is an early architectural discussion to get technical feedback from people working on Cosmos SDK, IBC, ZK systems, and interchain security. 1. The idea Imagine a user moving ATOM from Cosmos Hub to Osmosis. Today, the public source and destination transactions are observable, along with the relevant IBC packet information. With VeilRoute, the proposed flow would be: Cosmos Hub / Other IBC Chain | IBC Deposit | v +---------------+ | VeilRoute | | | | Shielded Pool | | ZK Validation | | Private Notes | | Audit Records | +---------------+ | IBC Withdrawal | v Destination IBC Chain Users would deposit an IBC asset, shield it into a private not
events.headline: [Discussion] VeilRoute: An IBC-Native Confidential Routing Chain with Threshold-Governed Disclosure

events.excerpt: Should the Cosmos Hub have its own price oracle? CosmWasm is now permissionless on the Hub, but there is no price oracle available to contracts. Pyth dropped CosmWasm, SEDA is EVM-only, and Band over IBC is slow and costs fees on every query. Without prices, we can’t build any advanced defi on the Hub. So these apps get built on chains like Injective or dYdX, and ATOM ends up used everywhere except on its own chain. Idea: integrate an enshrined oracle based on the Slinky fork. Validators would publish prices at every block, secured by the Hub’s own validator set, with no dependency on an external provider. And beyond the Hub: these prices could be distributed over IBC to any connected chain that lacks an oracle. The Hub would become an interchain’s price provider, with fees flowing back to ATOM stakers. Longer term: prices are only the first step. The same validator-voted mechanism could later carry other data the interchain needs, such as LST exchange rates, proof of reserves or other verified off-chain data. The Hub would become the interchain’s trusted data layer. The Community Pool could fund the development and audit. Would you support this direction? Validators, would you be willing to run an oracle sidecar? 20 posts - 7 participants Read full topic
events.headline: Oracle on Cosmos Hub

Users can now also choose their own history pruning point with --history.chain <block number>:<block hash> . It works both for pruning an existing node with geth prune-history and for snap sync, which then skips downloading the chain history before that block. events.excerpt: This is a maintenance release with accumulated bug fixes and improvements, and is recommended for all users. It continues the implementation work for the upcoming Amsterdam hardfork. A few things worth highlighting: The default GOGC has changed from 20 to 50, trading a higher memory peak for less GC overhead. Set --gogc=20 to keep the old behavior. Pebble v2 is now supported as a key-value store backend. Pebble v2 is used when Geth is bootstrapped from scratch, and falls back to Pebble v1 for a pre-existing database. Run geth db pebble-upgrade to explicitly upgrade a legacy Pebble v1 database to v2. Fork Implementation Several Amsterdam EIPs have been implemented or updated: EIP-2780: Resource-based intrinsic transaction gas ( #35212 , #35318 ) EIP-8037: State creation gas cost increase ( #35173 , #35318 , #35301 , #35342 , #35279 ) EIP-8038: State-access gas cost update ( #35216 ) EIP-8246: Remove SELFDESTRUCT burn ( #35219 ) EIP-8282: Builder execution requests ( #35175 , #35341 ) EIP-7997: Deterministic factory contract ( #35223 , #35285 ) EIP-7954: Increase maximum contract size ( #35217 ) EIP-7928: Block-level access lists ( #35260 , #35281 , #35261 , #35348 , #35279 ) Improve Amsterdam fork test coverage ( #35364 ) Introduce the --override.amsterdam flag ( #35213 ) Remove n

events.excerpt: Lord Ranger is a Member of the UK House of Lords and serves as Co-Chair of the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) on Digital Markets and Digital Money. Opinions below are his own. At a pivotal moment for the future of money, last week an evidence session with the Bank of England offered something we do not often get: a clear, candid readout from the heart of the UK’s monetary authority on how it views digital assets, systemic stablecoins, and the digital pound. After 18 months deeply engaged in the digital assets regulatory debate, as co-chair of the APPG on Digital Markets and Digital Money, I came away with two overriding impressions: the Bank is listening, and the Bank is cautious. Both are understandable. Neither, on their own, will be sufficient. Let’s start with the positive. The tone of engagement matters, and it is improving. The Bank’s willingness to absorb and reflect on feedback, particularly on its consultation into systemic stablecoins, is both genuine and welcomed. This is not a regulator operating in isolation; it is one actively trying to understand how innovation is unfolding in real time. That matters because stablecoins are no longer theoretical. events.headline: Lord Kulveer Ranger on digital assets, digital pound, and stablecoins

events.excerpt: Developers behind Solana-based derivatives exchange Drift proposed on Tuesday a recovery plan that would funnel protocol revenue to users who lost money in a devastating April hack. The developers also proposed relaunching the protocol before July “a leaner, perps-native exchange with an emphasis on security.” “The Drift team is taking considered measures to ensure that users are made whole, and that Drift restores itself as the leading perpetuals DEX on Solana,” they said in an update posted on the exchange’s website. “The team has made internal hard decisions to restructure and operate as lean as possible, focusing entirely on recovery and relaunch.” But various elements of the recovery plan will have to be approved by Drift tokenholders — and, if all goes according to plan, victims could wait years to break even. On April 1, hackers were able to trick Drift administrators into approving bogus transactions. The hackers made off with crypto worth $295 million, forcing Drift to suspend trading and other activity. Blockchain analysts have since said North Korea was likely behind the hack. events.headline: Drift to issue ‘recovery tokens’ in wake of $295m hack

Decentralised finance is notorious for being home to some pretty wacky ideas with dubious commercial viability. Yet over the past year, developers have stumbled on one that not only works, but also happens to be quite profitable: letting users buy and sell virtual versions of trading cards. Onchain marketplaces that allow users to speculate on the prices of Pokémon, One Piece, and sports cards have soared over the past year. They generated a combined $11 million in revenue last month, according to data from DefiLlama, generated on its new Pro dashboard . Revenue on DeFi TCG marketplaces is up more than 9X year-over-year, with top marketplaces generating over $11M in April. The success comes as trading cards — particularly Pokémon — continue their popularity. Nostalgia, financial speculation, and a post-pandemic boom in collectibles have caused prices to soar in recent years. events.headline: DeFi rides Pokémon trading card boom as onchain marketplaces bring in $11m

events.excerpt: Coinbase just cut 700 jobs. But Wall Street is liking what it sees. Coinbase shares popped as much as 4% early on Tuesday morning after the flagship US crypto exchange announced it was slashing about 14% of its global workforce in a sweeping restructuring that refocuses the company around artificial intelligence. CEO Brian Armstrong broke the news in an email to employees, citing two punishing forces: a reeling market still down about $1.5 trillion from its peak, and AI. "Over the past year, I've watched engineers use AI to ship in days what used to take a team weeks," Armstrong wrote in the email, which he reposted on X. "Non-technical teams are now shipping production code and many of our workflows are being automated." “We’re fundamentally changing how we operate: rebuilding Coinbase as an intelligence, with humans around the edge aligning it,” he added. As of December 31, Coinbase had 4,951 employees, according to its 2025 financial report . Based on that figure, the exchange's 14% job cut impacts 693 employees. The move puts Coinbase in company with Meta, which is cutting roughly 10% of its workforce, and Microsoft, which is trimming headcount through a voluntary retirement programme. Across many high-flying tech companies, the logic has been the same. The exchange expects t
events.headline: Coinbase shares pop as CEO Brian Armstrong cuts 700 jobs and blames AI

events.excerpt: The digital cooperative governing Uniswap, the biggest decentralised exchange, is voting on a proposal to take back some $42 million worth of governance tokens from delegates. Between 2022 and 2023, Uniswap’s decentralised autonomous organisation, or DAO, loaned out 12.5 million UNI to the nonprofit Uniswap Foundation and several top delegates in a bid to boost governance participation. According to Erin Koen, the proposal’s author and governance lead at Uniswap Labs, the protocol’s governance is now much more active, meaning that the loaned tokens have served their purpose. “Today, Uniswap’s governance environment looks very different,” Koen said. “UNI holders have been actively delegating voting power, and since DUNI was established, passed proposals have averaged roughly 75 million votes in turnout, exceeding quorum by approximately 88%.” DUNI, Uniswap’s Decentralized Unincorporated Nonprofit Association, is a legal entity that recognises onchain governance votes as legally binding and shields DAO members from personal liability for collective decisions. Truly decentralised? The proposal to take back the loaned tokens comes as Uniswap Labs and the Uniswap Foundation work to address criticism that the protocol’s governance system isn’t as decentralised as it appears to be. Crit
events.headline: Uniswap DAO votes to take back $42m of governance tokens loaned to delegates

The decentralised finance exchange processing $6 billion in daily derivatives volume launched its first outcome contracts over the weekend — and the early numbers turned heads, according to Hyunsu Jung, CEO of Hyperion DeFi. Its first Bitcoin outcome market did roughly three times the volume of equivalent markets on Polymarket and Kalshi combined, Jung told DL News. “This proves that having a shared liquidity layer is effective in converting users,” he said. "Binary markets is an obvious next step in building the full financial stack on Hyperliquid, which is meaningfully dominating crypto perpetuals and in the first half of 2026 has demonstrated the possibilities of 24/7 real-world asset trading.” Hyperion DeFi is a US publicly-traded company that accumulates Hyperliquid's HYPE token. Shares of the world's largest corporate Bitcoin holder have surged more than 50% over the past month, riding the top crypto’s climb past $80,000 as short sellers scramble for the exits and institutional money pours back in. events.excerpt: An emergency hearing on Wednesday could determine whether the relatives of a slain minister are entitled to $71 million in crypto that was nearly stolen by North Korean hackers last month. The hearing, scheduled by a federal judge in New York, is part of a fast-moving legal skirmish that has complicated an industry-wide effort to compensate the victims of an April 18 hack allegedly executed by North Korean hackers. That exploit saw hackers make off with nearly $300 million in rsETH stolen from the Kelp DAO protocol. The hackers then used the stolen crypto as collateral to borrow other, more liquid assets on Aave, the largest protocol in decentralised finance. But several organisations were able to freeze some of the stolen crypto before it could be laundered. Arbitrum DAO was the most successful, freezing crypto worth about $71 million. Arbitrum DAO is poised to send that crypto to a recovery fund meant to compensate users affected by the hack. But other people who have been victimised by North Korea are now trying to claim the frozen assets, citing decade-old, multimillion-dollar legal judgments against the pariah nation. events.headline: Aave secures emergency hearing to void ‘catastrophic’ restraining order

events.excerpt: A version of this story appeared in The Guidance newsletter on May 4. Sign up here. Christmas came early for the US crypto industry on Friday evening, when Punchbowl News reported that Senators had struck a deal limiting the payment of interest or yield on stablecoins. Reactions ran the gamut. Crypto investor Nic Carter said , simply, “The banks won.” Attorney Scott Johnsson, general counsel at Van Buren Capital, was more optimistic. “This is fine,” he wrote on X. “It may not feel like it, but it is.” But there was only one that really mattered. “Mark it up,” Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong wrote , seemingly signalling his support for a markup — a committee vote that could advance the bill. The odds the Clarity Act passes in 2026 quickly jumped from 46% to 64% on Polymarket. Recall that Armstrong single-handedly put the bill on ice back in January, when he pulled his support on the eve of a scheduled markup. Armstrong said he was unhappy with the bill’s treatment of stablecoins, among other things. Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott postponed the markup, and negotiators went back to the table. Notably, other crypto executives appeared unhappy with the decision. Last year’s stablecoin legislation, the GENIUS Act, banned stablecoin issuers from paying yield or interest on custom
events.headline: Clarity Act odds surge on stablecoin compromise, Coinbase support

events.excerpt: A California-based cannabis vape pen company that says it rewards customers with crypto for using its product is raising alarm among health experts and anti-drug campaigners. Gudtrip advertises itself as building a user-powered network that combines cannabis, Bitcoin, and artificial intelligence. “Every hit earns crypto,” a tagline on the company’s website reads. Customers who buy one of the company’s cannabis vape pens can connect it to an app, which rewards them with Bitcoin, and points for using the pen. “Checking-in” daily creates streaks which increase points earned by up to 200%. Several researchers studying cannabis consumption who spoke to DL News said encouraging daily use is potentially dangerous and habit-forming, raising ethical concerns. “Gamifying cannabis use? It certainly sounds like habit-formation is the goal,” Joshua Gowin, an associate professor who studies the effects of frequent cannabis use at the University of Colorado Anschutz, told DL News . “Linking a reward to a puff/smoking session reinforces the behaviour, increasing the chance of escalating use and even developing an addiction,” Janna Cousijn, head of the Neuroscience of Addiction Lab at the Erasmus University Rotterdam, told DL News . “It is potentially a very dangerous and unethical device that co
events.headline: ‘Every hit earns crypto’? App that gives users Bitcoin for getting stoned deemed ‘dangerous’ and ‘unethical’

events.excerpt: Ethereum's core developers have delivered their most significant technical milestone in months, emerging from a week above the Arctic Circle with a credible roadmap to dramatically scale the network's capacity. Last week, just over 100 core contributors gathered in Longyearbyen, on Norway's Svalbard archipelago — some 78 degrees north, where the sun never sets — for the Soldøgn interop, a week of intensive work on the Glamsterdam network upgrade. By Friday, the team had locked in a post-Glamsterdam gas limit floor of 200 million, stabilised external block builder implementations, and finalised gas repricing numbers for EIP-8037. "At their best, interop weeks can compress a month of asynchronous progress into each day," Ethereum Foundation researcher Tim Beiko wrote in a recap shared with developers on Friday. The breakthrough lands as Ether trades at $2,377, still more than 50% below its August peak of $4,946. However, signs of hope are emerging. Ethereum has jumped 14% over the past month, CoinGecko data shows . The 200 million gas limit target is notable because it determines how many transactions Ethereum can process per block. The higher the limit, the more activity the network can handle without congestion — and the stronger the case for Ethereum as the backbone of a global
events.headline: Ethereum devs huddled in the Arctic Circle to fix the network. Here’s what to know

events.excerpt: Bitcoin punched through $80,000 on Monday, up 19% over the past month, as a twin engine of institutional demand and legislative momentum roars back to life. On the first day of May alone, $630 million poured into US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, extending a two-month winning streak that made April the best month since October, DefiLlama data shows . ETF inflows have become the dominant force behind Bitcoin’s ascent, Max Kahn, CEO of investment adviser Digital Wealth Partners, told DL News . They now act as “an increasingly important source of consistent buying pressure,” helping the asset hold higher levels as long as institutional appetite remains intact. The institutional surge comes as Washington closes in on a legislative breakthrough. Senate Banking Committee chair Tim Scott told Fox Business on Friday that the Clarity Act — the landmark digital asset market structure bill — is heading for a bipartisan markup in May and a Senate floor vote soon after. ‘Red zone’ "We're in the red zone," Scott said, signalling the bill is nearing the Senate floor and that each procedural step strips away regulatory fog that has long restrained institutional capital. “I just want to have thirteen of thirteen Republicans on board,” he said. “That makes it easier for us to have a bipartisa
events.headline: Bitcoin tops $80,000 price as Clarity Act nears Senate floor with new Fed chair imminent

events.excerpt: Crypto companies raised just over $600 million from venture investors in April, DefiLlama data shows . That’s despite the epidemic of “disingenuous innovation” that is plaguing the digital assets industry, Diego Martin, CEO of Yellow Capital, told DL News , referring to grand promises widely made by crypto startup teams that are rarely fulfilled. “Institutional investors typically wait for retail demand before taking a punt on innovation,” Martin said. To be sure, fundraising in April fell some 75% from March, which was a blockbuster month that saw massive raises in the prediction market sector amid a shifting focus in the crypto industry. “Trust is the primary barrier — and opportunity — to tap into, due to the nature of the technology we work with,” Martin said. Still, marquee investors including German banking giant Deutsche Börse Group, Andreessen Horowitz, Paradigm and Coinbase, all piled on capital into crypto companies including Kraken, OpenGradient , and Pixie Chess . These are the top three raises in April. Kraken, $200 million Payward, the parent company of crypto exchange Kraken, raised $200 million through a secondary share sale to Deutsche Börse. The deal gives the German banking group a minority stake as it moves deeper into digital assets. The move values Kraken at
events.headline: Crypto companies raised $600m in April despite despite market downturn, VCs say

events.excerpt: April was a bad time for the crypto industry. Over the past month, 29 crypto projects have suffered hacks or exploits, the highest monthly tally in the industry’s history, per DefiLlama data. Among them were two standouts: The hacks of Solana-based exchange Drift, and Ethereum-based restaking app Kelp DAO, which resulted in a combined $579 million loss. The situation has sparked a crisis of confidence among the industry’s most ardent believers and left them questioning whether the tradeoffs inherent in decentralised technology are worth the trouble. In recent years, the number of crypto hacks — and the amounts stolen — have edged higher. The fast-moving and experimental DeFi space, once notorious for exploits, was thought to have matured. But now it’s back in the limelight — and not for the right reasons. “Right now, DeFi seems to be the primary target,” Michael Pearl, vice president of strategy at crypto security firm Cyvers, previously told DL News . “In general, everything has shifted now to hacking humans rather than hacking systems.” Single points of failure The problem, according to Michael Egorov, founder of DeFi protocols Curve Finance and Yield Basis, is centralisation. “We need to reduce the number of single points of failure as much as possible,” Egorov said in a state
events.headline: Crypto industry reels as April sees highest number of hacks ever

events.excerpt: Bitcoin just got a war upgrade. On Thursday, US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth told Congress that Bitcoin projects inside the Pentagon are “classified and ongoing,” while stressing that the top crypto is a tool for American power. Hegseth delivered the comments in front of the House Armed Services Committee, responding to questions about whether the US is securing a strategic advantage in technology. “I am a long enthusiast of Bitcoin and crypto potential,” he said. “A lot of the things we are doing, enabling it or defeating it, are classified efforts that are ongoing inside our department, which do provide us a lot of leverage in a lot of different scenarios.” Hegseth’s endorsement elevates Bitcoin into the realm of geopolitical strategy at a time when Russia and China are expanding their roles in mining and using digital assets to bypass US sanctions. As rival powers lean on crypto to settle energy trades and reduce dependence on the dollar amid geopolitical turmoil, Washington’s embrace signals that Bitcoin is now part of the global balance-of-power conversation. Still, Bitcoin’s price has not budged. The top crypto is down some 40% from its October peak of $126,000 even as the S&P 500 and other asset classes blaze record highs amid investor optimism. Hegseth himself has long b
events.headline: Hegseth recasts Bitcoin as national security asset amid Russia, China expansion

events.excerpt: Artificial intelligence is a Sword of Damocles dangling over crypto — but Wall Street isn’t quailing, says Coinbase. Anthropic’s new Claude Mythos AI model is able to exploit security vulnerabilities autonomously and therefore threatens crypto markets, according to a second-quarter outlook by Coinbase and Classnode. In theory, it could hammer key weak points across protocols, exchanges, and infrastructure. But that’s not shaking institutional investors’ confidence in Bitcoin, David Duong, Coinbase’s global head of investment research said in a note shared with DL News. He highlighted that three‑quarters of institutions “still see Bitcoin as undervalued” despite the short-term fears clouding the market’s sentiment. Duong’s confidence comes as crypto has struggled to keep up with other asset classes like stocks or gold. Bitcoin is still down nearly 40% from its October peak while the S&P 500 printed a new record in April. It is currently trading at $77,000 after rallying some 13% over the past month. “Our outlook for the next quarter remains neutral, but there are early signs the market may be finding a floor,” Duong said. “Much of the speculative activity has been flushed out.” Exchange-traded fund inflow data backs him up. events.headline: Anthropic’s new Mythos AI will hit crypto. Bitcoin investors don’t care, says Coinbase

events.excerpt: The US Senate voted unanimously to ban prediction market trading among Senators and their staffers on Thursday. The Senate joined several other organisations that have banned employees from trading on the platforms to avoid conflicts of interest. Last week, Illinois Governor JB Pritzker banned state employees from using insider information to bet on prediction markets. A day earlier, National Public Radio issued a similar directive to its editorial employees. "Serving in Congress is an honor, not a side hustle," Senator Bernie Moreno, a Republican from Ohio and the bill's sponsor, said in a statement on X. "Americans deserve to know that their leaders are here for the right reason!" The resolution approved by senators on Thursday changes the chamber's rules, and violations are policed by its members. It does not have the force of law, and it does not need to be approved by the House of Representatives or signed by the president. The resolution comes as bills to regulate prediction markets flood Congress. Ritchie Torres, a New York Representative, presented the Public Integrity in Financial Prediction Markets Act of 2026 in January to block federal officials from trading on prediction markets. In March, Democratic senators Jeff Merkley and Amy Klobuchar filed a bill to formally pr
events.headline: US Senate bans prediction market trading by Senators, staff

events.excerpt: A pair of US Senators are demanding answers from Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick after a recent news report raised questions about his relationship with Tether, the world’s largest stablecoin issuer. A trust benefitting Lutnick’s four children borrowed from Tether in October, just as Lutnick sold them his multibillion-dollar stake in finance giant Cantor Fitzgerald, Bloomberg reported last month. Lutnick’s stake in Cantor Fitzgerald was reportedly sold to multiple trusts that benefit his children. But the trust that borrowed from Tether holds more than half the equity in Cantor, according to Bloomberg. Moreover, the loan was reportedly backed by “all assets” in the trust. “If reports of this loan are accurate, it would raise serious questions about your relationship with Tether and the company’s influence on your policy decisions,” Senators Elizabeth Warren and Ron Wyden wrote in their letter, dated April 29. “We want to ensure that Tether has not sought to bribe or otherwise exert control or influence over you.” Tether and the Department of Commerce did not immediately respond to DL News’ requests for comment. The letter is the latest example of Democrats using crypto as a cudgel against President Donald Trump and his allies, many of whom have ties to the industry. Democrats a
events.headline: Democrat Senators question Howard Lutnick over Tether ties

events.excerpt: MegaETH’s token is off to a shaky start. On Thursday, the layer 2 blockchain, which lists Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin among its early investors, launched its MEGA token, airdropping some 500 million tokens to those who bought them during the project’s October public token sale. The token began trading at 11 am London time and initially rose to an all-time high of $0.38, according to CoinGecko data. But it quickly began to sell off, dropping some 55% to trade at around $0.17. Despite the volatility, those who bought the token during the public sale are still in profit. MegaETH sold the tokens at a clearing price of $0.0999 each, raising just under $50 million. The project also sold 500 million tokens via a $10 million funding round on Echo, the early stage investing platform, at $0.02 each. MegaETH’s wobbly launch comes as investor appetite for new crypto tokens dwindles. The crypto market has been in the lurch since October, when it experienced a huge, structural crash that triggered over $19 billion in leverage liquidations. Since then, investors' interest has been mostly limited to established cryptocurrencies, such as Bitcoin.
